GET /api/reports/data/m365-inactive-acco.summary: Inactive Microsoft 365 accounts, by client and tenant
GET /api/reports/data/m365-inactive-acco.description: Every account brought in by the Microsoft 365 sync that nobody signs in to, with the client it maps to and the tenant it came from. Options: inactiveDays (default 90, 1–730), includeDisabled and includeUnknown (both default true), tenantId for one connected tenant, plus clientId from the shared report filters. An account with no sign-in activity recorded is reported as unknown rather than inactive, and the payload says so in `notes` — reading it needs Entra ID P1 and AuditLog.Read.All on the app registration. Requires report:view and integration:view.

GET /api/reports/data/billing-aging.summary: Receivables ageing, by bucket and by client
GET /api/reports/data/billing-aging.description: Every unpaid invoice (status `sent`, `partial` or `overdue`) aged in days past its due date into five buckets — not yet due, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90 and over 90 — with a per-client matrix of what each client owes in each bucket, the oldest debt per client and the 25 largest unpaid invoices. A point-in-time report: `from`/`to` are deliberately not applied, because what is owed is what is owed today, and `asOf` names the date the age was measured. The buckets come from the same definition the revenue summary uses, so `totals.outstanding` equals `revenue-summary`'s `totalOutstanding` for the same scope; `basis` returns the bucket rule and the statuses counted. Requires report:view and honours `clientId`.

GET /api/reports/data/billing-tax-summar.summary: Tax collected and taxable revenue, by rate, jurisdiction and client
GET /api/reports/data/billing-tax-summar.description: Tax collected and taxable revenue for the period (invoices by issue date, drafts excluded), grouped by rate, by jurisdiction and by client, with what was invoiced against what has been paid and what remains outstanding. The schema has no tax-jurisdiction column, so jurisdiction is derived from the client's billing country and state (falling back to its primary address) and any invoice whose client has neither is grouped as "Not recorded" rather than guessed — `basis` states this. Tax rates are stored two ways in this database (invoices as a percentage, service agreements as a fraction), so a rate above 1 is read as a percentage and one at or below 1 as a fraction; `dataQuality` counts invoices whose recorded tax does not equal subtotal x rate, invoices with a 0% rate, invoices with no jurisdiction and the drafts that were left out. Requires report:view and honours `clientId`, `from` and `to`.

GET /api/reports/data/billing-forecast.summary: Projected revenue from active agreements and recurring invoices
GET /api/reports/data/billing-forecast.description: Revenue projected forward from active service agreements and recurring invoices. `months` sets the horizon (1–24, default 6) and the window starts with the month after the current one. Each agreement is repeated at its recorded billing amount and cadence, anchored on its next invoice date (or its start date when none is set) and stopped at its end date; each recurring invoice is stepped by its own recurrence rule from its next generation date, and one that belongs to an active agreement is counted once, through the agreement. The answer carries a monthly series, the contribution of each agreement, what expires in the horizon, and `assumptions` — the whole basis, including that hourly and overage work is not projected, amounts are before tax, and no growth, churn or currency conversion is assumed. Anything that could not be projected is listed in `dataQuality` with the reason instead of being counted as zero. Requires report:view and honours `clientId`.

_README: Curated operation documentation, keyed by `METHOD /path` exactly as the router declares it.
scripts/generate-openapi.mjs merges these into docs/openapi.yaml; anything missing still appears
with a summary derived from its path, so this file is where a description is made *better*, never
where the document is completed. Add an entry when an operation's purpose is not obvious from its
path, when it is what an integrator will reach for, or when its behaviour needs a warning.

POST /api/auth/login.summary: Sign in and receive a session token
POST /api/auth/login.description: Email and password in, a bearer token out. When the account has a second factor the answer is an `mfaToken` instead, which POST /api/auth/mfa/verify exchanges for the real token — the response also names `mfaMethod` so a client shows the right challenge rather than always offering an authenticator field, and `rememberDays` so it only offers a "do not ask again" control when the deployment honours one. A browser that already proved a factor for this account's current enrolment is not challenged again and is signed in here, with the skip recorded. Every successful answer carries `mfaPolicy` (see GET /api/auth/mfa/policy), because an account can be signed in and still owe an enrolment the deployment now requires. A token is what the Authorization header carries for a person; a program should use an API key instead.

GET /api/auth/me.summary: The signed-in identity, with its permissions
GET /api/auth/me.description: The cheapest way for a client to confirm a credential works and to learn the permissions it holds.

GET /api/auth/client-ip.summary: The address this connection is arriving from
GET /api/auth/client-ip.description: Unauthenticated, because the sign-in screen asks before a session exists and this is the first fact worth having when a sign-in behaves oddly from a VPN, a proxy or a client's network. Answers with `req.ip` — the same value the session record and the audit trail carry — so the screen and the trail agree. How much of a forwarded header is believed is `TRUST_PROXY`: unset (the dev default) it is the socket address, while a deployment sets it to the number of proxies in front of the app (1 for the Container Apps ingress, 2 once Front Door precedes it), so there the address is the caller's rather than a proxy's. The rate limiter buckets on this same value. Nothing here is instance data: the caller is being handed their own address back.

POST /api/auth/mfa/verify.summary: Exchange an MFA challenge for a session token
POST /api/auth/mfa/verify.description: The second half of MFA sign-in: the mfaToken from POST /api/auth/login plus either a six-digit code from the account's authenticator app **or a single-use recovery code**, which is accepted in the same `code` field. A recovery code is spent by the attempt, so a second use of the same one is refused; the sign-in is recorded with a reason naming it, because a session that was opened with a recovery code is the most interesting row an administrator will read all week. Send `remember: false` to withhold the trusted-browser cookie; anything else grants one for the number of days the deployment configured, and a deployment configured to zero never issues one. The answer carries `mfaPolicy` so a client knows whether the account still owes an enrolment — the two are separate questions: this endpoint answers "is this the right person", the policy answers "have they done everything the deployment requires".

GET /api/auth/mfa/policy.summary: What this account owes, and which methods it may choose from
GET /api/auth/mfa/policy.description: One call that answers every question about the caller's second factor, so the enrolment wizard, the reminder banner and the account screen cannot disagree about the deadline. The answer resolves the instance settings against the account's own row and returns the conclusion rather than the settings: `enabled`, `mode`, the methods actually offered, the method this account enrolled, whether it is `required`, whether it `mustEnrolNow`, and — while a grace period is running — `graceUntil` and `daysLeft`. `catalogue` lists every method this build supports with `offered` resolved for this deployment (**not** the same question as `available`: an unoffered method is reported rather than hidden, because "why can I not use my passkey" is what the screen exists to answer) and `governedBy`, the configuration section and field that decides it — passkeys are governed by `sessions.passkeys`, so a screen can say where to change it instead of offering a control it cannot honour. `enforcementPossible` reports whether the deployment's current settings permit requiring a second factor at all.

POST /api/auth/mfa/enrol/email/start.summary: Email an enrolment code to the signed-in account
POST /api/auth/mfa/enrol/email/start.description: Sends a fifteen-minute code to the address on the caller's own account, so somebody who cannot install an authenticator app can still satisfy a requirement. Distinct from POST /api/auth/send-mfa-email, which continues a **sign-in** that has already proved a password and carries an `mfaToken`; this one belongs to a session that is already open. Refused with `403` when the deployment does not offer emailed codes, and answers `502` when the relay rejects the message — a code nobody can read is worse than a visible failure, so the caller is told not to wait for it. Requires a session. Rate limited with the credential endpoints.

POST /api/auth/mfa/enrol/email/verify.summary: Finish enrolling an emailed code as the second factor
POST /api/auth/mfa/enrol/email/verify.description: Completes the enrolment begun by POST /api/auth/mfa/enrol/email/start: the code is compared in constant time, and on success the account is marked enrolled with `email_code` as its method, the pending code is cleared and any grace deadline is satisfied. A code that has expired is refused with a message saying so rather than a generic failure. Requires a session.

GET /api/api-keys/permissions.summary: Every scope a key may be issued with
GET /api/api-keys/permissions.description: The permission catalogue, so a client can build a key without hard-coding scope names, plus the purposes a key can be labelled with (rmm, siem, flexpoint, quickbooks, monitoring, scheduler, other).

GET /api/api-keys.description: Names, prefixes, scopes, owner, last use and state — never the secret and never its hash. `?includeRevoked=true` keeps the history.

POST /api/api-keys.summary: Issue a key for a program
POST /api/api-keys.description: The only time the secret is returned — store it in the client, and revoke the key if it is lost. The key acts as `userId` (the caller by default), intersected with `permissions`, so it can never exceed the account it borrows.

POST /api/api-keys/:id/rotate.summary: Issue a new secret for the same key
POST /api/api-keys/:id/rotate.description: Scopes, owner and name stay; the previous secret stops working immediately.

DELETE /api/api-keys/:id.description: Recorded as a state rather than a deletion, so the inventory keeps its history. Requests using the key are refused from the next call.

POST /api/events.summary: Receive an event from another system (RMM, SIEM, monitoring)
POST /api/events.description: The gateway every outside system sends to. Idempotent by (source, externalId): a repeat attaches to the ticket the first event opened and counts the occurrence, and `kind: recovery` closes that ticket instead of opening one. Needs ticket:create. Returns what happened — whether a ticket was opened, joined or closed — rather than only that the request was understood.

GET /api/events.summary: Recently received events, with the ticket each became
GET /api/events.description: Filter with ?source= and ?state=open|recovered. Useful for answering "did the RMM reach us?".

GET /api/events/sources.summary: Which systems have sent events, and how many

POST /api/flexpoint/sync.description: Reads customers, invoices and deposits according to the connection's options, stores them, links customers to clients, and records settled payments when that option is on. The same work the Sync button on C7NC → FlexPoint does. A scheduler can call this on a timer: FlexPoint publishes no webhooks, so nothing arrives on its own.

GET /api/flexpoint.summary: The FlexPoint picture: connection, options, counts, client receivables
GET /api/flexpoint.description: Everything the configuration page is drawn from, and the cheapest way to read a client's receivable in bulk.

PUT /api/flexpoint/options.description: What to pull, how customers are matched to clients, whether clients are created for unmatched customers, whether the client id is written back, whether settled payments are recorded, and whether invoices may be pushed. Writes to FlexPoint or to the ledger are off until switched on.

POST /api/flexpoint/link.summary: Tie a FlexPoint customer to a client, or untie it
POST /api/flexpoint/link.description: One customer per client — linking replaces any previous one. `customerId: null` clears the link without touching FlexPoint.

GET /api/flexpoint/clients/:companyId.description: Open balance, overdue, what has been received, the invoices FlexPoint holds, and the FlexPoint payments recorded here.

POST /api/flexpoint/invoices/:invoiceId/.summary: Create or update this invoice in FlexPoint
POST /api/flexpoint/invoices/:invoiceId/.description: Refused unless "push invoices" is switched on for the connection. Idempotent: an invoice that already carries a FlexPoint id is updated rather than created twice.

GET /api/flexpoint/invoices.summary: Local invoices with their FlexPoint state

POST /api/cloudconnect.description: kind, name, credentials and settings. `GET /api/cloudconnect/types` publishes what each connector needs, including the field labels and explanations the configuration dialog shows.

GET /api/cloudconnect/types.description: Every connector kind, what it does, the credentials it needs (with labels, hints and the vendor's own API reference) and the settings it honours.

POST /api/cloudconnect/:id/test.description: A real call to the provider. On failure the answer names the fields at fault and how to fix them.

POST /api/cloudconnect/:id/sync.description: For FlexPoint this runs the full FlexPoint sync (linking and payments included); for every other kind it stores what the adapter returned.

GET /api/cloudconnect/:id/synced-entitie.summary: What a connector has brought in

GET /api/cloudconnect/status.description: State, detail, when it was last verified and whether it is stale, without calling the provider.

POST /api/tickets.description: The same ticket a person would open, with the fields an integrator needs: board, client, contact, priority, assignee. The response carries the `ticketNumber` it was given — `{boardCode}-{client}-{count}`, e.g. `MSP-04-1005`, where the middle part is the client id minus 1000 and the last is that client's ticket count, so it is not a global series and not something to build on: read it back, do not predict it. Prefer POST /api/events for monitoring traffic — it is idempotent, and this is not.

requestExample.title: Printer offline
requestExample.description: Reported by the client's office manager.

GET /api/tickets.description: Filtered and paginated. A client-scoped credential only ever sees its own client's tickets.

PATCH /api/tickets/:id.summary: Update a ticket, including closing it
PATCH /api/tickets/:id.description:
Status, priority, assignment, board and the rest. A status change emails the ticket's contact — that is what the notifications are — so two fields exist to control it. `closeNotes` is the reason the ticket is being closed: it is written to the (customer-visible) thread and it is what the closing email says. `notifyCustomer: false` does the same work in silence, for a ticket whose contact has gone or one closed by mistake.

**Omitting `notifyCustomer` is not the same as sending it**, on a status change that settles the ticket: an absent value means the caller has no opinion and the ticket's board decides, via `notifyCustomerOnClose`. That is how a board whose tickets arrive from monitoring systems at no-reply addresses stays quiet. An explicit `true` or `false` always wins, in both directions.

Closing settles the ticket (`closed`, `resolved`, `cancelled`) and emails the client a message that invites a reply. A reply from one of the client's own contacts reopens the ticket as `customer_reopened` and puts it back in the queue — the reply itself is recorded on the ticket before the status changes.

requestExample.closeNotes: Replaced the failing switch and confirmed the link is stable.

POST /api/tickets/:id/comments.summary: Add a note or reply to a ticket
POST /api/tickets/:id/comments.description: `isInternal: true` keeps the note off the customer's copy, which is what an integration's working notes should be.

GET /api/clients.description: The client list, filterable by status, type, territory and search.

POST /api/clients.description: Only `name` is required. This is what the FlexPoint option "create clients for unmatched customers" calls internally.

GET /api/billing/invoices/:id/pdf.summary: An invoice, drawn as a printable page
GET /api/billing/invoices/:id/pdf.description: The invoice as a **standalone HTML document** — not JSON — ready to print or save as a PDF: a white A4 or Letter sheet with 18 mm margins, the instance's letterhead from `brandForDocument("invoice")`, an unambiguous date format, the money block, a pay block and a footer with page *n* of *m*. Deliberately self-contained: the CSS is inlined because the page is fetched on its own, and a document is not a screen, so it never follows the user's theme. The amount due is the balance the **payments** make it, so a part-paid invoice states what is outstanding rather than the gross total; when the recorded status and the recorded payments disagree, the payments win and the page says so. `taxRate` is read with the repo's convention — above 1 it is a percentage, at or below 1 a fraction — so an invoice recording 8.5 prints `Sales tax · 8.5% · US · IL` and not `Tax (850.0%)`. An invoice with no `InvoiceLineItem` rows states the agreement its amount came from instead of printing an empty table over a live subtotal. Requires billing:view and the client scope the caller already carries; a company-scoped account gets 403 for another client's invoice.

GET /api/billing/clients/:companyId/stat.summary: What a client owes, aged, as a printable page
GET /api/billing/clients/:companyId/stat.description: A statement of account as a **standalone HTML document** — not JSON — on the same paper as the invoice: every invoice issued to the client and still open, listed with its age and its ageing band, and totalled by band (not yet due, 1–30, 31–60, 61–90, over 90). Each row's **balance** is its total less the payments recorded against it, which is the figure that cannot be wrong: the overdue-reminder email states `invoice.total` as the outstanding balance, so a part-paid invoice is chased for the wrong amount there. Pass `?invoice=<id>` to narrow the document to one invoice — the shape the reminder email attaches — while keeping the same figures and the same ageing. 404 when the invoice named is not this client's. Requires billing:view plus a scope that includes the client.

POST /api/billing/invoices/generate.summary: Generate an invoice from unbilled time

GET /api/quotes/:id/pdf.summary: A quote, drawn as a proposal you can print
GET /api/quotes/:id/pdf.description: The quote as a **standalone HTML document** — not JSON — on the same paper as the invoice and the statement. A quote is an offer, not a demand, so it is shaped differently on purpose: it states what is proposed before it shows a price, says the day the price stops being true, and ends with three ways to answer — accept, ask, or book — plus a signature line for acceptance. There is no expiry column on `Quote`, so a validity written in the quote's own `notes` ("Valid for 30 days.") is honoured and labelled as such, and thirty days from the day the quote was prepared is the fallback, labelled as a convention rather than a record. Whole-router gate: with the `billing.quotes` flag off the route answers 404 like the rest of this router. Requires billing:view and a scope that includes the quote's client.

POST /api/billing/invoices/:id/send.summary: Send an invoice to the client

POST /api/billing/invoices/:id/record-pa.summary: Record a payment against an invoice

POST /api/billing/batches/:id/approve.description: Issues every draft in the batch and offers each invoice to the connected accounting system. When the connection is FlexPoint and pushing is allowed, that push goes through FlexPoint's merchant API.

GET /api/service-alerts.description: What the alert banner and the Outage Board read.

GET /api/alert-webhooks.description: Where this application sends service_alert.raised and service_alert.resolved, with the signing secret and which events each endpoint wants.

POST /api/alert-webhooks/:id/test.summary: Send a test delivery to a webhook

GET /api/console/catalog.summary: The console commands this credential may run
GET /api/console/catalog.description: The command catalogue, grouped the way `help` prints it and filtered by the caller's own permissions at call time, so a client is told what *it* can run rather than shipped a list it will be refused. Every command names the route it runs and the permission that route checks; the console itself has no permission, and authorizes nothing — it builds the same request the screen builds and lets the route decide (PLAN-028 §6). Reads only: the write commands arrive with PLAN-026's action manifest. `counts.total` is reported beside `counts.available` so a caller can see what its account is missing without being told what it contains. Answers 404 when the console is switched off for the deployment.

GET /api/console/catalog/:name.summary: One console command, with its flags and its route
GET /api/console/catalog/:name.description: A single descriptor, for `c7ntax help <command>` and for tooling. The name is the command as typed (`ticket show`), so it is URL-encoded; `+` is accepted for the space. A command the caller's credential may not run is 404, not 403: the catalogue is filtered rather than guarded, and not being offered a command is indistinguishable from it not existing — which is the same rule the record lookups follow.

GET /api/alert-webhooks/deliveries.summary: What was delivered, and what failed

GET /api/system/changelog.summary: What's New — the release notes as structured data

GET /api/system/version.summary: The version the running build identifies as
GET /api/system/version.description: The newest entry of the same notes `/changelog` returns, without the change history: for labelling the application itself — the account menu shows the build beside the logo — and for answering "what is this deployment running?" in one request. Parsed once and re-read only when BuildNotes.md changes, so the label costs nothing per page load. `version`, `date` and `title` are null on a build whose notes cannot be read, rather than a 404: an unknown version is a state a client can render, not an error worth logging.

GET /api/system/audit-logs.description:
Actions with their actor, entity and timestamp. This is the join an SIEM wants: correlate a detection with the change someone made after it.

Two optional filters, both of which only narrow the result. `mine=true` limits the rows to the caller's own — narrower than the unfiltered read this route has always served, and what the header's Recent activity menu asks for, so a caller is never shown a colleague's activity under the word "mine". `limit` caps the page (default 500, maximum 500): the audit screen wants hundreds of rows and a menu wants five.

`entityId` is the record the action touched where the route had one. For a creation that is the id of the row the route returned, so a created record can be linked to; for a route with no id in its path it is the last path segment, which for a collection is the collection's name (`clients`) and for an action is the action (`generate`) — so a client reading this should treat a non-id `entityId` as "the operation or the collection", not as a record.

GET /api/configuration.description: Every setting the application reads: value, source (default, environment, or saved), what changing it affects, and what it defaults to.

GET /api/portal/tickets.summary: The customer portal's own ticket list
GET /api/portal/tickets.description: Portal routes are authenticated by a contact's one-time code, not by a staff session — they are listed here so the surface is complete, not as something an integration should call.

GET /api/kb.description: The published articles, with /api/kb/drafts for the ones not published and /api/kb/categories for the tree.

GET /api/reports/:id/run.summary: Run a report and get its rows
GET /api/reports/:id/run.description: The custom report designer's runner: a stored template rendered against live data, returning the rows and the totals it computed.

GET /api/dashboard/layout.description: Per-user, not global: this is the arrangement of the widgets on the caller's own dashboard.

GET /api/oauth-app.summary: What the OAuth app wizard needs before it starts
GET /api/oauth-app.description: The permissions a deployment will request (`Mail.ReadWrite` as an application role, `Mail.ReadWrite`/`User.Read`/`offline_access` delegated), the redirect URI this instance must be registered with for the delegated flow, the default registration name, and the by-hand command that does the same thing from a terminal. `integration:manage`.

POST /api/oauth-app/start.summary: Begin a deployment: a device code for the tenant administrator
POST /api/oauth-app/start.description: Starts the OAuth device-code flow against Microsoft's public Graph command-line client, so nothing about the tenant is held here and the administrator signs in themselves. Returns the code to type and the URL to open; poll the session until it is authorised. The tenant may be a GUID or a primary domain, and a tenant that does not exist is refused by name.

POST /api/oauth-app/import.summary: Read the script's output (or the four values) instead of deploying from here
POST /api/oauth-app/import.description: The offline path through the wizard, for a tenant this instance cannot reach the Microsoft sign-in endpoint, or a registration that already exists. Paste the contents of `O365/out/c7ntax-m365-app.json` in `scriptJson`, or send `tenantId`/`clientId`/`clientSecret`/`mailbox` directly. Refuses a client id that is not a GUID, and refuses a registration granted `Mail.Read` instead of `Mail.ReadWrite` — the connector marks messages read, so read-only connects and then fails on the first message.

warnings: Confirm the Exchange Online scoping commands were run: until they are, an app-only registration can read every mailbox in the tenant.

POST /api/oauth-app/:sessionId/poll.summary: Has the administrator approved the sign-in yet?
POST /api/oauth-app/:sessionId/poll.description: Asks Microsoft. Answers `pending` while the code is unapproved (and lengthens the interval if Microsoft says `slow_down`), `authorized` once a token has been granted — with the account and tenant id read from that token's claims — or `declined`/`expired` with the reason. Deploying before this says `authorized` is refused with 409.

POST /api/oauth-app/:sessionId/deploy.summary: Create or reuse the registration, grant consent, mint the secret
POST /api/oauth-app/:sessionId/deploy.description: The same sequence as `O365/New-C7NTAXMailboxApp.ps1`, over Graph: find or create the application by display name (an existing one is *reused*, not duplicated), record `requiredResourceAccess` with the application role id of `Mail.ReadWrite` (and the delegated scope ids plus the redirect URI when the delegated flow is wanted), create the service principal consent is granted *to*, grant admin consent with all three ids, and create a client secret for 12 months unless the flow is delegated (which uses PKCE and must not have one). Also returns the Exchange Online commands that scope an app-only registration to one mailbox — Graph has no route to those. The secret is returned once and never stored by this API; the audit row keeps the expiry instead.

warnings: Confirm the Exchange Online scoping commands were run: until they are, an app-only registration can read every mailbox in the tenant.

GET /api/oauth-app/:sessionId.summary: Where a deployment got to, without contacting Microsoft
GET /api/oauth-app/:sessionId.description: The session's own state: pending, authorized, declined, expired or failed, plus the tenant, mode, mailbox and display name it was started with.

GET /api/roles.summary: Every role, and the one role only a Super Admin is shown
GET /api/roles.description: The role inventory with how many people wear each one. Two things are withheld from a caller who is not a **Super Admin**: the **Developer Admin** role is not returned at all, and `developer:view` and `developer:purge` are removed from every role's permission list — including a custom role that was deliberately given one. A Super Admin sees all of it. The same rule governs `GET /api/roles/:id`, which answers `404` for that role rather than returning it, so a single fetch is not a way around the list. Requires `role:manage`.

PATCH /api/roles/:id.summary: Rename a role, change its type, or set its permissions
PATCH /api/roles/:id.description: Only the fields sent are changed. A caller who is not a Super Admin is **refused with the offending key named** — `Refused: developer:view. Only a Super Admin may see or set the Developer Admin role and the developer permissions.` — when the submitted permission list contains `developer:view` or `developer:purge`, when the target role *is* the Developer Admin role, when the edit would move a role onto `developer_admin`, or when the role already holds one of the two keys. That last case is refused rather than accepted because those keys are not returned to that caller, so honouring the edit would quietly withdraw a permission they were never shown; a rename of such a role is refused for the same reason. A Super Admin is unrestricted. Requires `role:manage`.

GET /api/users.summary: The user directory, without the accounts on the developer surface
GET /api/users.description: `search`, `role`, `status`, `limit` and `offset` as usual. The accounts wearing the **Developer Admin** role are excluded for a caller who is not a Super Admin, and excluded **inside the query** rather than filtered out of the page: `total` counts only what the caller can see, and `?search=` cannot reach one. Every picker built on this endpoint — assignees, approvers, managers — inherits the same answer. Requires `user:manage`.

PATCH /api/users/:id.summary: Edit a person: profile, placement, status, role, permissions
PATCH /api/users/:id.description: Only the fields sent are changed; a role or permission change needs `role:manage` **and** can never be applied to your own account. An account wearing the **Developer Admin** role may only be changed by a Super Admin: every write to one from anybody else is refused, by name — `Refused: devadmin@example.com. Only a Super Admin may see or change an account on the Developer Admin role.` — whether it edits the profile, activation, the password, MFA, the role or a permission override. `GET /api/users/:id`, `DELETE /api/users/:id`, `POST /api/users/:id/lock`, `POST /api/users/:id/reset-password` and `POST /api/users/:id/reset-mfa` answer the same way, and the single fetch answers `404` instead, so an id learned elsewhere is not a way round the directory. Requires `user:manage` (`security:manage` for the two reset routes).

PATCH /api/users/:id/mfa.summary: Say whether one account has to have a second factor
PATCH /api/users/:id/mfa.description: The per-account half of the MFA policy, and the answer to "everyone except this one". `state` is `default` (follow the instance setting), `disabled` (exempt from a requirement — an account that has already enrolled keeps being asked for its factor, because this exempts it from being *required* to have one, not from having one) or `enforced` (required whichever way the instance setting is set). The words are Entra's on purpose: an administrator who has used Entra already knows them. **Requiring is not enrolling** — nothing here touches what the account has set up, and an account that is required but has not enrolled is given the configured grace period rather than stopped on the spot, so the answer includes the resolved `policy` for the target. Moving an account to `disabled` clears any deadline it was given, since the countdown no longer applies. Requires the `mfa:enforce` permission, which is what that permission was declared for.

GET /api/security/sign-ins.summary: The sign-in log: every attempt, and how it ended
GET /api/security/sign-ins.description: Newest first, filterable by `result` (`success`, `failure`, `locked`, `mfa_failed`, `code_failed`, `signed_out`), `userId`, a `from`/`to` window and a `search` across the address, device, IP address and reason. The `summary` beside the rows counts the whole **filtered** set, not the page, so "how many of these were lockouts" is answerable per window. Each row names the `method` — password, authenticator app, emailed code, passkey, single sign-on or portal code — which is what separates "signed in" from "signed in with a second factor". A row is written for every way in and for signing out, successes included, and `userId` is null when the address typed was not an account. Events about an account on the **Developer Admin** role are withheld from a caller who is not a Super Admin — by account *and* by address, because a row records what was typed and can be written with no `userId` at all — and the `summary` is counted over the same filtered set. A row whose address is not an account at all still reads, because what it holds is what somebody typed. Requires `security:manage`.

GET /api/security/sessions.summary: Who is signed in right now
GET /api/security/sessions.description: One row per browser session with the person, the device read from the user agent, the `method` that opened it (from the sign-in event, not the session row), the address it arrived from, when it started and when it was last seen. `state` is `active` (the default), `ended` or `all`. Sessions belonging to an account on the **Developer Admin** role are withheld from a caller who is not a Super Admin, and `?userId=` for one narrows to nothing rather than being replaced by the rest. Requires `security:manage`.

DELETE /api/security/sessions/:id.description: Stamps `invalidatedAt` rather than deleting the row: the session keeps saying what happened, and the cookie it belonged to stops resolving on the next request. Revoking one that has already ended answers `{ "revoked": false }` rather than failing. A session belonging to an account on the **Developer Admin** role is refused to a caller who is not a Super Admin, by name. Requires `security:manage`.

POST /api/security/sessions/revoke-user.description: Ends every live session a user has, for the day a laptop is lost or a password is suspected leaked. Body is `{ "userId": "…" }`; the answer is how many sessions were ended. Changing a password or disabling an account already does this, so it exists for when neither has happened and it is needed now. An account on the **Developer Admin** role is refused to a caller who is not a Super Admin, by name. Requires `security:manage`.

GET /api/security/devices.description: Passkeys (which sign in) and browser notification subscriptions (which receive), each with the account it belongs to, when it was registered and when it was last used. Filter with `userId`. Both kinds are *added* by the person they belong to, so this is the half an administrator needs: seeing a device nobody recognises, and a path to a lost phone. A device belonging to an account on the **Developer Admin** role is withheld from a caller who is not a Super Admin, and `?userId=` for one narrows to nothing. Requires `security:manage`.

DELETE /api/security/devices/passkey/:id.description: Deletes the credential, so the device can no longer sign in as that person. The recovery path for a lost phone as much as the response to a device that should not be there — the account holder can also do it themselves, under My Settings → Security. Removing a credential from an account on the **Developer Admin** role is refused to a caller who is not a Super Admin, by name. Requires `security:manage`.

DELETE /api/security/devices/push/:id.description: Deletes the browser's push subscription, so alerts stop arriving there. Separate from the passkey route because it deletes from a different table: a mistake in a shared handler would be a mistake in both. Removing a subscription from an account on the **Developer Admin** role is refused to a caller who is not a Super Admin, by name. Requires `security:manage`.

GET /api/email-connectors.summary: Every watched mailbox, and the board it files into
GET /api/email-connectors.description: One row per watched address, which is the mapping: `alerts@` files to the NOC board, `servicedesk@` to the service desk. Each row carries its transport and health — last poll, messages processed, last error — so a mailbox that has stopped working is visible without opening it. Secrets are never returned: `hasPassword`, `hasClientSecret` and `hasRefreshToken` say whether one is set.

GET /api/email-connectors/m365-apps.summary: The Microsoft 365 apps, the addresses on each, and how to scope them
GET /api/email-connectors/m365-apps.description: Connector rows grouped by registration, because one app usually watches several addresses and Exchange scopes it per mailbox rather than per app. Each app comes back with every address on it, the board each one files into, and `scopingCommands`: the Exchange Online commands that cover all of those addresses at once — one management scope and one role assignment each. The service principal's object id is not stored (it belongs to the deployment), so the commands say so rather than inventing one. Requires `integration:view`.

POST /api/email-connectors.summary: Watch another mailbox, and choose the board it files into
POST /api/email-connectors.description: Takes the Microsoft 365 app inline (`tenantId`, `clientId`, `clientSecret`) or names an existing connector to copy it from with `reuseAppFromConnectorId` — the tenant, application id and secret are copied from that row, so a second mailbox on the same app needs only `user` and `boardId`. The secret moves as stored ciphertext and is never shown again; a `clientSecret` sent alongside a reuse is ignored rather than stored. `boardId` and, for an app-only Graph connector, `user` are required; a new connector is created **disabled** so it can be tested before it starts turning mail into tickets. Requires `integration:manage`.

POST /api/tickets/batch.summary: Apply one change to many tickets
POST /api/tickets/batch.description:
Status and priority only. `notifyCustomer: false` closes a batch without emailing anybody, which is usually what housekeeping wants; `closeNotes` is recorded on every ticket in the batch. Note that closing a batch *does* email each ticket's contact, one ticket at a time — there is no digest.

Omit `notifyCustomer` and the board decides **per ticket**, because a single selection can span boards: a NOC ticket stays quiet while the ones beside it are told. Send `true` or `false` and that answer is used for all of them.

In the application, a batch that includes **Close** stops and asks first (email the client, or close in silence) rather than closing in the background: the request below is what that dialog sends, not what a ticked checkbox sends on its own.

GET /api/procurement/orders.description: Filtered by `status` and `vendorId`, newest first, with each order's vendor and lines included. Nothing here is client-scoped: a purchase order is ours, not a customer's.

GET /api/procurement/orders/:id.description: The record rather than the row: the lines as ordered (with the catalog SKU where a line came from the catalog), the vendor's own details, who raised and who approved it, and the four dates that say whether it is late — created, ordered, expected, received.

POST /api/procurement/orders.description: `vendorId` is required and the number is generated (`PO-?`). Totals are computed from the lines, so `subtotal` sent by a caller is ignored.

PATCH /api/procurement/orders/:id.summary: Move a purchase order along, or re-price it before it arrives
PATCH /api/procurement/orders/:id.description:
`status` is one of `draft`, `ordered`, `shipped`, `received`; moving to `ordered` stamps `orderedAt` and moving to `received` stamps `receivedAt` unless a date is sent, so a late delivery can be recorded as the day it actually arrived. `expectedAt` and `notes` are editable at any point.

**Receiving an order writes the asset inventory**: one asset per unit, named from the line, tagged `{poNumber}-{line}-{unit}`, priced at the line's cost and carrying the order number, unassigned until somebody puts it at a client. The reply's `assets.created` says how many were written; one line is capped at 25 records and the remainder is added to the order's notes rather than dropped; re-receiving the same order writes nothing twice.

`lineItems` replaces the lines and recomputes `subtotal` and `total` from them — refused once the order is `received`, because a receipt is a record of what arrived and a line list that can change afterwards is not one. A status moved back from `received` clears `receivedAt`.

PATCH /api/procurement/vendors/:id.description: The details that end up on a purchase order: who to contact, how to reach them, the payment terms that decide when their invoice is due, and the tax id it has to match.

GET /api/developer/environment.summary: What this instance is configured to be
GET /api/developer/environment.description: Every environment name the application declares — the ones the configuration registry names as the variable a setting replaces, and the ones the API reads directly — reported as `set` or falling back to the declared default, with the value in force where it is safe to print it. **A secret is never returned**: a name that looks like a credential reports `set`, `secret: true`, `withheld: true`, `effective: null` and a `hint` (the last characters of a fingerprint, enough to confirm *which* value is in place), and the payload says so in `secretsWithheld`. Beside it, `badge` names the instance (NODE_ENV, whether that means production, the host and port, the app version, the git commit where it can be read), `flags` is the flag registry as read-only rows with what is saved and what the environment alone would give, and `settings` is the effective value of every declared setting grouped by configuration section. Requires `developer:view`, which only the `Developer Admin` role holds.

GET /api/developer/purge/preview.summary: What a purge would remove — and what it would leave standing
GET /api/developer/purge/preview.description: A dry run with real counts, in three lists. `removed` is `WIPE_MODELS` (85 tables, counted in the child-before-parent order `db:sample-off` deletes them, each with a `why`), `preserved` is `KEEP_MODELS` (13 tables: identity and platform configuration, so the instance stays usable), and `unlisted` is the third list this endpoint exists for — models `apps/api/prisma/schema.prisma` declares that **neither** list names, and which therefore *survive* a purge. That is not a defect in the lists: it is the fact an operator has to see before pressing the button, because data outliving a "purge" is how a demo tenant reaches production. `dryRun` totals the removed figure, `auditRows` says how many rows of `auditLog` are inside it (the purge takes the trail too), `snapshot` describes the manifest a purge would replace (`locked` when the sample dataset is already off), `disabled` says whether it is already off, and `requiredPhrase` is the exact string `POST /api/developer/purge` will accept — returned rather than hard-coded on the screen so the two cannot drift. Requires `developer:view`.

POST /api/developer/purge.summary: Purge the sample data, exactly as db:sample-off does
POST /api/developer/purge.description:
Body: `{ phrase, reason }`. **Refused with 400 unless the phrase matches `requiredPhrase` exactly and the reason is a sentence** — a `details` list names which field failed (`phrase`, `reason`), and the message says so too. Refused with **409** when the sample dataset is already disabled (the CLI returns quietly in that state; a route that did would answer 200 for an act that did not happen) and when a purge is already running.

What it does is `pnpm db:sample-off`'s own code path, called rather than re-implemented: take a snapshot, delete `WIPE_MODELS` children-before-parents, then set `.sample-data-disabled`. While that marker is set the snapshot is **locked** — automatic snapshot capture and the automatic reseed after a change both stop — and `pnpm db:sample-on` is what clears it and reseeds. `KEEP_MODELS` and the unlisted models are untouched, so the instance stays usable but not empty of everything an operator might expect.

**The receipt is the record, and it is written where the purge cannot reach it.** The purge deletes `auditLog`, so the audit row is written *after* the wipe and the durable copy is a `SystemConfig` row under the reserved `sample_data:` prefix, which the general configuration endpoint refuses to every caller including administrators. The response names it in `receiptPath` and `wrote`, and carries who, when, why, the phrase, the dry-run figure, the rows and tables removed, and the snapshot taken. A purge takes as long as the snapshot capture takes, so a client may give up before the answer arrives — the work continues and the receipt is still written. **Requires `developer:purge` *and* `developer:view`**, chained rather than listed together: `developer:view` alone cannot purge, and neither Super Admin nor Admin holds either permission.

requestExample.reason: Clearing the demo dataset before the first production deployment.

GET /api/developer/health.summary: The repository's own guards, as they answer on this working copy
GET /api/developer/health.description: Runs the repository's check scripts — `check-route-guards`, `check-api-docs`, `check-config-reads`, `check-console-catalog`, `plugin-metadata check`, `audit-baseline`, `check-encoding`, `check-help-links`, `lint-design-tokens` — as child processes from the repository root, and reports each with its command, its own output (`detail`) and how long it took. Status is one of **three** words: `pass`, `fail`, or `skip` — and a check that could not run (its script is not on this working copy, the tool it needs is not installed, or it ran out of time) is `skip` with the reason, *never* a pass. A failing check never fails the request: the failure list is the answer, and an HTTP 500 instead of "plugin metadata: fail" would hide the thing the panel exists to show. On this tree `guard:plugin` fails and `guard:deps` needs `pnpm audit`, so it may not run at all. Requires `developer:view`.

GET /api/developer/deployment.summary: Where the deployment stands against PLAN-030
GET /api/developer/deployment.description:
The Azure go-live plan with a surface: eight steps — target and naming, parameters and secrets, infrastructure, database, the readiness gate, network and ingress, sanitisation, and validate-and-hand-off — each with whether it is shared or Azure-specific, a state drawn from five values (`done`, `attention`, `blocked`, `decision`, `unverified`), what the step decides, the commands that run it, and a checklist whose every item names the evidence its state was decided from and what happens if it is skipped.

**Derived where it can be, `unverified` where it cannot.** An item whose answer is in this repository is decided by reading it — the migrations that exist, whether a deployment switch is set, whether TLS verification is on, the database name, whether the API has a readiness endpoint and whether both promotion gates ask it, whether the parameter file still carries a placeholder. Everything else is `unverified` with the reason, and nothing in this package has met an Azure subscription (said in `plan.unverified` and in `unread`). The two open items — `webOrigin` still a placeholder, and the app connecting as the server administrator — come back as `blocked`/`attention` rather than green, and the last High item, the least-privilege database role, is a `decision` deferred by the operator rather than a forgotten finding. Also carries the four advisories, the four decisions the operator owns with their recommendation, the §8.11 go-live bar, and a hand-off summary. Requires `developer:view`.

POST /api/developer/deployment/records.summary: Record the answer to a decision or a check
POST /api/developer/deployment/records.description:
Body: `{ kind, id, note }` — `kind` is `decision` or `check`, `id` is one of the ids the report itself names under that kind (a decision such as `2.3`, or a checklist item such as `5.1`), and `note` is what was decided. **Refused with 400 naming the field that failed**: an unknown `kind`; an `id` this report does not name — or names under the *other* kind, so a checklist id submitted as a decision is refused rather than filed against the wrong list; and an empty `note`, because a record that names nothing is a record nobody can act on and it would sit in the payload looking like an answer. The refusals are a `details` list as well as a message.

**Recording is not destructive**, so this needs `developer:view` like its siblings and deliberately not `developer:purge`: deciding what to do about the ingress is not the same act as emptying the database.

**Where the answer is kept.** One record per subject, in `SystemConfig` under the reserved prefix `deployment:record:<kind>:<id>` — the same mechanism the purge receipt uses, and reserved in `routes/system.ts` beside `sample_data:`, so no HTTP caller can read or rewrite one (administrator included) and **a purge never touches it**. A decision taken before a purge is a decision that survives it, which matters because the purge is one of the things a decision may be about. Recording again **replaces** the answer rather than stacking a second one; the reply is `201` when the subject had no answer and one was created, `200` when an earlier answer was replaced.

The response is the **whole payload `GET /api/developer/deployment` would have returned** — including the updated records — plus `saved` naming the record just written, so a screen re-renders from one response instead of a write followed by a read. On the GET, every recorded answer appears three ways: in `records`, and attached to its own decision or checklist item as `record`. A record whose subject the report no longer names is still returned in `records` — a check that lost its id is exactly when somebody needs to read what was decided about it.

requestExample.note: Front Door Premium alone, with a Private Link origin. Agreed with the operator.

GET /api/email/messages.summary: Every message this instance can send, with what fires it and who reads it
GET /api/email/messages.description: The trigger matrix: one entry per EmailMessageKey, with its group, its audience (customer or internal), its editing class, whether it is live, what fires it, the recipient rule the code enforces today, the files it may carry, the merge fields it may use, and the template currently in force. `counts.customised` is the question this screen exists to answer — which of these have we changed? — and `counts.neverSent` counts the senders nothing calls. The recipient rule is returned read-only and deliberately: who receives a message is a fact about the ticket, not a word in the template, so the person editing can see who will read what they are writing. Requires email:view. The two dead senders (`ticket.closure`, `invoice.send`) and the two reserved keys (`report.scheduled`, `quote.send`) appear here marked `live: false` rather than being hidden, because a well-formed email with no caller is exactly the thing that must not be mistaken for a delivered one.

GET /api/email/templates/:key.summary: One message's template, its state, and the plain text derived from its blocks
GET /api/email/templates/:key.description: The template as the editor wants it: subject, blocks, the stored plain-text part (`text`, null when it is derived rather than written), and `derivedText` — the text the blocks produce, which is what is sent when nobody has edited the text part. `state` is `default` when the stored words are the ones the code ships, `customised` when they are not; a template that has never been edited reads as `default` with version 0 and no row behind it. `derivedText` is rendered against the sample records so the two parts can be compared side by side; a preview against a real record is POST /api/email/preview. Requires email:view.

PUT /api/email/templates/:key.summary: Change what a message says, keeping the previous version
PUT /api/email/templates/:key.description: Saves the subject, the blocks and (optionally) a hand-written plain-text part, and writes an `EmailTemplateVersion` row for the state being replaced, so the history panel and its reset have something to return to. The version is bumped on every save and every send records the version it used, so the delivery log can answer "which words did the customer actually get" after the template has moved on. Passing `text: null` means "derive it from the blocks", which is the default. Refused with 400 when the subject is empty, when a block is not one of the thirteen kinds in the shared vocabulary, or when the save would drop a token the message cannot be without — `auth.mfa_code`, `user.invite` and `portal.login_code` are the codes somebody is waiting for, and the API refuses a version of them that no longer carries it rather than storing an email that cannot do its job. Requires email:manage.

blocks.html: We are still waiting on your reply, and this ticket has been idle for {{message.idleFor}}.

GET /api/email/templates/:key/versions.summary: The saved versions of a message, newest first
GET /api/email/templates/:key/versions.description: Up to 50 versions, each with its subject, blocks, plain-text part, when it was saved, who saved it and the note they gave. Version 0 is not in the list: it is the built-in default in the code, which is what "reset to default" returns to. Requires email:view.

POST /api/email/templates/:key/reset.summary: Put a message back to the words the code ships
POST /api/email/templates/:key/reset.description: Overwrites the stored template with the built-in default and records that as a new version, rather than deleting the row: the version history is what makes a reset safe to perform, and deleting the template would cascade it away. The message then reads as `state: default`. Requires email:manage.

POST /api/email/preview.summary: Render a message against a real record, without sending or storing anything
POST /api/email/preview.description: Body: `key`, an optional `subject`/`blocks`/`text` draft so an unsaved change can be seen, and a `target` of `{ kind: "ticket" | "invoice", id }` or `{ kind: "sample" }` to use the named records from the seed. Returns `subject`, `html`, `text` and `derivedText`: both parts come back deliberately, because the owner asked for a message that is still readable when a mail system strips the markup and the only way to be sure of that is to look at the text part. `warnings` names what a person approving the message should know first — a merge field the record cannot supply (it renders as a stated absence rather than as a blank that changes a sentence's meaning), a link that is in the HTML and not in an edited text part, or a condition the sender could not answer. This is the same renderer every live send and POST /api/email/templates/{key}/test use, so the preview is the message rather than a likeness of it. Requires email:view, and sends nothing.

POST /api/email/templates/:key/test.summary: Send a real message to one address and log it
POST /api/email/templates/:key/test.description: Body: `to` (one address), an optional `target` of the same shape POST /api/email/preview takes, and optional `subject`/`blocks`/`text` so what is on screen can be sent before it is saved. The message is rendered, sent, and written to the delivery log with `test: true` so a test is never mistaken for a message a customer received. Answers 502 when the relay refused it, naming the reason — the send path itself never throws, but this is the one place where "it did not go" is something somebody is standing in front of and needs to read. Requires email:manage, because it sends mail to an address of the caller's choosing.

GET /api/email/brand.summary: The brand kit every message is measured against
GET /api/email/brand.description: The stored values, plus `effective` — what a message actually uses, defaults included — and `smtpFrom`, the address the API was started with, so a screen can show what an unset sender identity falls back to rather than an empty box that means something. One row for the instance, shared with the PDF letterhead rather than being a second brand for email. Requires email:view.

PUT /api/email/brand.summary: Change the brand kit: colours, assets, footer, legal line and sender identity
PUT /api/email/brand.description: Colours must be hex values (`#c00000`), and the sender and reply-to addresses are validated. A blank `fromEmail` means "whatever `SMTP_FROM` the API was started with", which is what every message uses until somebody sets one. The banner and button colour come from `primaryColor`; the `signature` and `footer` blocks draw `companyName`, `productName`, `footerText` and `legalText`, so a change to the sign-off is one change rather than one per message. Requires email:manage.

requestExample.footerText: Sent by C7NTAX on behalf of Cyber 7 Group, LLC.

GET /api/email/log.summary: What left the building, what failed and why, and which version of the words was used
GET /api/email/log.description: Newest first, with `key` to filter to one message, `limit` (default 50, maximum 200) and `offset` for paging, plus `counts` for sent, failed and test. Every row carries the template key and the version that went out — so "which words did the customer actually get" is answerable after the template has moved on — the provider's own message id, the outcome, and the reason when it failed. Nothing in this product logged a send before this table existed. Requires email:view.

GET /api/brand.summary: The instance's identity, and what each kind of document wears
GET /api/brand.description: One read for the whole Branding section, because its four subjects are four views of one record. Returns the identity ? product and company name, tagline, the letterhead logo and its dark variant, the square icon, the wordmark, the contact line and postal address, the website, the two colours, the document footer and legal text, and the email sender ? plus `documents`, one row per document family with its presentation already resolved (family default, then what is stored) and a `changed` flag; the fixed document `palette`; and `contrast`, the ratio of each settable colour against paper with the `minimum` a printed mark needs. `documentPresentation` is the raw stored map, and `effective` is what every send actually uses with defaults applied. Requires branding:view.

PUT /api/brand.description: Partial semantics that matter: a field **absent** from the body is left alone, a field present and blank clears it, so a screen that owns only part of the record cannot empty somebody else's field. `documentPresentation` is a map keyed by document family. Colours are refused unless they are a three- or six-digit hex value, and the sender and reply-to addresses are refused unless they parse as addresses. Writes an audit row. Requires branding:manage.

POST /api/brand/assets.summary: Upload a logo or an icon
POST /api/brand/assets.description: Takes `{ kind, dataUrl }` where `kind` is `logo`, `logoDark` or `icon` and `dataUrl` is what a browser's FileReader produces, and answers `{ id, url, contentType, byteSize }` with 201. PNG, JPEG or WebP only ? **SVG is refused**, because an uploaded SVG is a script with an image's extension ? and 2 MB. The bytes are checked against their own magic number rather than trusted from the request, so a renamed file cannot be stored as an image and served back. The returned `url` is `/api/brand/asset/<id>`: put it in `logoUrl`, `logoDarkUrl` or `iconUrl` and save. Requires branding:manage.

GET /api/brand/asset/:id.description: The stored bytes of one upload, with its content type, cacheable immutably ? a new upload is a new id, so a cached mark can never be stale. **Deliberately public**, and the only route in this API that is: a logo is an image inside an email and on a printed page, so it must be fetchable by a mail client that holds no session here, and serving it from the database by an opaque id means there is no filename to trust and no directory to traverse. It also sends `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin`, which is required rather than generous ? the document it appears on is fetched from this API and rendered by the web app, so the image is cross-origin by construction.

GET /api/brand/clients.summary: Each client's own brand, or what it inherits
GET /api/brand/clients.description: Every active client with its brand patch already resolved and an `inheritedLogo` marker, which is `portal` when the client has no logo of its own and is therefore wearing the one on its customer portal ? one client, one logo. Requires branding:view.

PUT /api/brand/clients/:companyId.summary: Give a client its own branding on the documents addressed to it
PUT /api/brand/clients/:companyId.description: Saves a patch over the instance's identity ? the case-by-case half of branding, for a client that is its own legal entity and must be invoiced under its own name and address. Every field is optional and an absent or null field means "the instance's own", so a client whose form was never filled in produces exactly the document it produced before. An empty patch clears the override. Requires branding:manage.

GET /api/brand/reports.summary: The reports whose appearance differs from their family's
GET /api/brand/reports.description: Only the rows that exist, each with its patch and who last changed it. The catalogue of reports is code and stays code ? its figures are the report ? so this deliberately does not return a stubbed row per report, which would be inventing content a person could then 'reset'. The settings screen already holds the catalogue and marks the overridden ones. Requires branding:view.

PUT /api/brand/reports/:reportKey.description: A patch on top of the report's family: title, subtitle, paper size, orientation, letterhead, the basis block, footer, page numbers and a footer note. Precedence is the order of specificity ? the family's stored settings, then a client's override, then this, which is how one report can print landscape while its family prints portrait. An empty patch deletes the row and returns the report to its family's default. Requires branding:manage.

GET /api/analytics/catalogue.summary: The measure catalogue: what each figure on the analytics screen means
GET /api/analytics/catalogue.description: The definitions behind the Analytics workspace: every measure with its label, group (service, responsiveness, effort, money, experience, commercial), unit, the sentence describing what it means and what it does not, which direction is good news, its target where one exists, and the endpoint and field it is read from. Also returns the measure groups and the four breakdown dimensions. The definitions live here rather than being written on the screen so that a figure and its explanation cannot drift apart, and the `source` field is a claim that can be checked: every measure is computed by a builder that already serves a standard report. Requires report:view.

GET /api/analytics/overview.summary: Every measure for one period, with the period's own limitations
GET /api/analytics/overview.description: Twenty-one measures computed from the same builders the standard reports use, in one round of queries rather than nine screens. Each measure returns its value, a sentence saying what the number means for this period, and a tone derived from its target; a measure with no target is neutral rather than good, because no target means no claim. `limitations` carries the data-quality sentences the builders themselves report - a period with no date range cannot produce a utilisation percentage, entries without a rate make recorded value a floor, and a period where no technician carries a cost rate makes every margin read high - so the screen can state why a figure should not be trusted rather than showing a percentage that is 100% because nothing was measured. A measure that cannot be computed is returned as null with the reason in its reading. Honours from, to, clientId and boardId through the shared report filters, and can only narrow the caller's own scope. Requires report:view.

GET /api/analytics/breakdown.summary: The same figures cut by client, board, technician or priority
GET /api/analytics/breakdown.description: Takes `dimension` (client, board, technician or priority; anything else falls back to client so a stale bookmark still opens) plus the shared report filters, and returns the tickets per group. For the client dimension it also joins the client-value report and returns a 0-100 account-health score with the reasons behind it: how old the oldest open ticket is, how much of the load is high priority, how much of what was invoiced is still out, and whether anything has been collected. A score is returned as well as a band because with a uniformly aged backlog every client reads the same band and the column stops carrying information. health, score and reason are null for the dimensions that have no client economics behind them, rather than inventing a band. Requires report:view.

GET /api/analytics/funnel.summary: Cash realisation: worked, billable, invoiced, collected
GET /api/analytics/funnel.description: The same delivered work at each step it can leak, assembled from three reports rather than recomputed: effort from time-tracking, value from technician-utilization, billing and collection from contract-profitability. Each step returns its value and a `leak` sentence naming what was lost between it and the previous step - hours recorded as non-billable, agreement hours that carry no rate and so can never become revenue, and the amount invoiced and not yet collected. The invoiced and collected steps are agreement-scoped, which `reading` states, because hours delivered against agreements are the part of the funnel that has a price attached. Requires report:view and honours the shared report filters.
